"Return of the Mack" is a song written and performed by British R&B singer-songwriter Mark Morrison, released by WEA Records as the third single from his debut album, Return of the Mack (1996). Produced by Morrison with Phil Chill and Cutfather & Joe, the song received positive reviews from music critics, appearing on Billboard magazine's "Top Songs of the '90s" and "500 Best Pop Songs of All Time" lists in 2019 and 2023, respectively.

Released in the United Kingdom on 4 March 1996, "Return of the Mack" topped the UK Singles Chart for two weeks the following month. The song then became a hit in Australia and Europe, entering the top 10 in multiple countries. In January 1997, it was released in the United States and reached number two on the Billboard Hot 100 that June, becoming Morrison's highest-charting hit in the US. The accompanying music video was directed by Jake Nava, featuring Morrison performing in an underground club.

sections.heading: Background and composition
sections.wikitext: The song's beat is [[Sampling (music)|sampled]] from the song "[[Genius of Love]]" by American band [[Tom Tom Club]].<ref>{{Cite magazine|last=Spitz|first=Marc|title=Tom Tom Club's "Genius of Love," a Hip-Hop Staple, Turns 30|url=https://www.vanityfair.com/culture/2011/01/tom-tom-clubs-genius-of-love-a-hip-hop-staple-turns-30|access-date=4 October 2020|magazine=Vanity Fair|date=10 January 2011|language=en-us}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last=Goodman|first=Lizzy|title=Tom Tom Club's Chris Frantz on 30 Years of 'Genius of Love'|url=https://www.vulture.com/2011/01/tom_tom_clubs_chris_franz.html|access-date=4 October 2020|website=Vulture|date=11 January 2011 |language=en-us}}</ref> "[[Games (Chuckii Booker song)|Games]]" by [[Chuckii Booker]] was also sampled, as well as fragments from "[[ESG (EP)|UFO]]" by [[ESG (band)|ESG]], "Rocket in the Pocket" by [[Cerrone]], and "Feel The Heartbeat" by [[Treacherous Three|The Treacherous Three]].<ref>{{Cite web|date=28 June 2016|title=Return Of The Mack: understanding the everlasting powers of Mark Morrison's classic|url=https://www.shortlist.com/news/return-of-the-mack-understanding-the-everlasting-powers-of-mark-morrison-s-classic|access-date=4 October 2020|website=Shortlist|language=en}}</ref>

sections.heading: Critical reception
sections.wikitext:
[[Larry Flick]] from ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'' magazine felt that UK crooner [[Mark Morrison]] "energizes a deflated U.S. [[Contemporary R&B|R&B]] scene" with the song,<ref>{{Cite web|first= Stephen Thomas |last= Erlewine |title= Mark Morrison – ''Return of the Mack'' |publisher= [[AllMusic]] |access-date= 10 November 2020 |url= https://www.allmusic.com/album/return-of-the-mack-mw0000089800 |author-link=Stephen Thomas Erlewine}}</ref> noting that he "shows international promise with fresh lyrics and vocals, and classic [[Soul music|soul]] production reminiscent of R&B's '80s heyday."<ref name="flick"/> Matt Diehl from ''[[Entertainment Weekly]]'' remarked that Morrison "comes off more like a funked-up [[Seal (musician)|Seal]], promising revenge to a deceitful lover in a warbly croon. The end result is an odd but infectious [[new jack swing|new-jack-swing]] variation on '[[Hey Joe]]', buoyed by bubbly beats and the insistent title refrain."<ref name="diehl"/> Another ''EW'' editor, Leah Greenblatt, described the track as a "new-jackalicious breakup jam".<ref>{{Cite magazine |first=Leah |last=Greenblatt |url=https://ew.com/article/2011/05/27/chart-flashback-1997/ |title=Chart Flashback: 1997 |magazine=Entertainment Weekly |date=27 May 2011 |access-date=27 February 2020}}</ref> Tom Ewing of ''[[Freaky Trigger]]'' noted that "the music certainly has his back – the rubbery basslines cocooning the song, the satisfying crunch of the drums, the light keyboard touches helping Morrison glide along his comeback trail." He added that it "is a pleasure to listen to, a well-tailored suit of sound."<ref>{{Cite web |first=Tom |last=Ewing |url=http://freakytrigger.co.uk/popular/2013/10/mark-morrison-return-of-the-mack/#debug5 |title=MARK MORRISON – "Return of the Mack" |work=[[Freaky Trigger]] |date=3 October 2013 |access-date=7 March 2020}}</ref>

Caroline Sullivan from ''[[The Guardian]]'' concluded in her album review, "He plays the sunglasses-at-night role to perfection on the album's title (and best) track".<ref>Sullivan, Caroline (26 April 1996). "Music: This week's Pop CD releases". ''[[The Guardian]]''.</ref> A reviewer from ''[[Music Week]]'' gave it four out of five, adding that the singer "looks to maintain the momentum of his hit 'Crazy' with another assured mix of R&B and [[ragga]]."<ref name="mw"/> Ralph Tee from the ''[[Record Mirror]]'' Dance Update gave it a top score of five out of five, writing, "This simply is every bit as good as what you would get from an American r&b act on a major label — and the song's better than most of what's coming out from across the pond of late." He added further, "The urban street production is a perfect vehicle for Mark's Jamaica-style tinged soul vocal on a song that deserves to be a smash, or an anthem at the very least."<ref name="tee"/>

sections.heading: Chart performance
sections.wikitext: "Return of the Mack" reached number one in the United Kingdom during its sixth week on the [[UK Singles Chart]], on 14 April 1996, and spent two weeks at the top.<ref name="uk"/> It entered the top 10 in Austria, Belgium ([[Flanders]] and [[Wallonia]]), Denmark, Germany, Ireland, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden and Switzerland, as well as on the [[Eurochart Hot 100]], on which it peaked at number five.<ref name="eurocharthot100">{{Cite magazine|url=https://worldradiohistory.com/UK/Music-and-Media/90s/1996/MM-1996-05-11.pdf|title=Eurochart Hot 100 Singles|magazine=[[Music & Media]]|volume=13|issue=19|date=11 May 1996|page=22|access-date=25 June 2018}}</ref> Outside Europe, "Return of the Mack" reached number one in Zimbabwe, number two in Australia, and number three in New Zealand. In North America, it peaked at number two on the US ''Billboard'' [[Hot 100]] and number 17 on the Canadian ''[[RPM (magazine)|RPM]]'' 100 Hit Tracks chart. It additionally topped the ''Billboard'' [[Rhythmic Top 40]] and ''RPM'' Dance charts. The single is [[Music recording certification|certified]] platinum or higher in Australia, New Zealand, the UK and the US.
sections.text: "Return of the Mack" reached number one in the United Kingdom during its sixth week on the UK Singles Chart, on 14 April 1996, and spent two weeks at the top. It entered the top 10 in Austria, Belgium (Flanders and Wallonia), Denmark, Germany, Ireland, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden and Switzerland, as well as on the Eurochart Hot 100, on which it peaked at number five. Outside Europe, "Return of the Mack" reached number one in Zimbabwe, number two in Australia, and number three in New Zealand. In North America, it peaked at number two on the US Billboard Hot 100 and number 17 on the Canadian RPM 100 Hit Tracks chart. It additionally topped the Billboard Rhythmic Top 40 and RPM Dance charts. The single is certified platinum or higher in Australia, New Zealand, the UK and the US.

sections.heading: Music video
sections.wikitext:
The music video for "Return of the Mack" was directed by British director [[Jake Nava]].{{citation needed|date=June 2026}} It begins with Morrison arriving in [[London]] by [[Concorde]] flight in the evening. In his car (a silver [[Mercedes-Benz SL-Class]]) travelling towards the city, he starts singing. He has flashbacks of himself and his girlfriend, now ex. The car then stops in front of his ex and her new boyfriend standing by the street. The singer sings as he watches the new couple. Later he arrives at an underground club and hands the DJ a record which is immediately played. Shortly afterwards, the ex shows up in the club with her new guy. Standing in the crowd of dancing people, Morrison sings towards his ex. Then (in a flashback of the breakup) he sits down at a desk, inside an office. The ex comes in and sits down. They are confronting each other, and she ends up getting up, letting the chair fall as she leaves, looking at Morrison with a regretful face. The video ends with a close-up of Morrison sitting in the office in thoughts, while he smiles to the camera.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Mark Morrison - Return of the Mack (Official Music Video) |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uB1D9wWxd2w |website=[[YouTube]] | date=23 June 2007 |access-date=22 September 2021}}</ref>

The ex-girlfriend is played by then unknown model Suzannah Agrippa miming to a featured vocal performance by [[Angie Brown]].<ref>{{Cite web|date=10 November 2020|title=The Number Ones Bonus Tracks: Mark Morrison's "Return Of The Mack"|url=https://www.stereogum.com/2103316/the-number-ones-bonus-tracks-mark-morrisons-return-of-the-mack/columns/the-number-ones/|access-date=8 November 2021|website=Stereogum|language=en}}</ref> Numerous other extras were friends of the director.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.complex.com/music/2016/03/return-of-the-mack-music-video-interview-jake-nava|title = Here's the Story Behind Mark Morrison's "Return of the Mack" Video| website=[[Complex Networks]] }}</ref>

sections.heading: Impact and legacy
sections.wikitext:
In December 1996, ''[[Melody Maker]]'' ranked "Return of the Mack" number nine in their list of "Singles of the Year", writing, "Forever playing in the mini-cab home, smooth and assured and absolutely f**ing diamond-sharp, Mark Morrison ruled supreme. The first great British [[Swingbeat|swing]] record."<ref>{{Cite magazine|url=https://www.flickr.com/photos/nothingelseon/53760986465/|title=Singles Of The Year|magazine=[[Melody Maker]]|date=21 December 1996|page=68|access-date=5 June 2024}}</ref> In 2007, ''[[Stylus Magazine]]'' ranked it number 40 on its list of the "Top 50 [[One-Hit Wonder]]s", stating that "over plush keyboards, fake turntable scratches, and a rhythm track that will be around 'til time immemorial, Morrison relates his griefs with an ex who he's returned to—what? Gloat in her face? Point out he's still surviving, even thriving? Nope, he's really returned to show what sleek [[Contemporary R&B|R&B]] grooves and odd vocal cadences he's developed since being dumped."<ref>{{Cite magazine |url=http://www.stylusmagazine.com/articles/weekly_article/stylus-magazines-top-50-one-hit-wonders.htm |title=Top 50 One Hit Wonders |magazine=[[Stylus Magazine]] |date=26 March 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080124143541/http://www.stylusmagazine.com/articles/weekly_article/stylus-magazines-top-50-one-hit-wonders.htm |access-date=29 August 2020|archive-date=24 January 2008 }}</ref> In August 2012, Polish ''Porcys'' ranked "Return of the Mack" number 71 in their list of "100 Singles 1990-1999".<ref>{{Cite web |title=100 Singli 1990-1999 |url=http://www.porcys.com/ranking/100-singli-1990-1999/3/ |website=Porcys |date=20 August 2012 |language=pl |access-date=2 April 2020}}</ref> 

In 2017, ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'' magazine ranked it number five in their list of "The 100 Greatest Pop Songs of 1997", writing, "From its first seconds, 'Return' busts through the wall like the [[Kool-Aid Man]], and just picks up stream from there, more undeniable in its boom-bap strut with each ''You liiiiiied to me'' braying and ''Once again!'' ad lib. Between this, [[Vanilla Ice]]'s '[[Ice Ice Baby]]' and [[Backstreet Boys]]' '[[Everybody (Backstreet's Back)]]', the '90s proved beyond a doubt that you don't need to be gone in the first place to have a triumphant banger proclaiming your return."<ref>{{cite magazine|first=Andrew|last=Unterberger|url=https://www.billboard.com/music/pop/greatest-pop-songs-1997-7849063/|title=The 100 Greatest Pop Songs of 1997: Critic's Picks|work=[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]|date=29 June 2017|access-date=7 November 2024}}</ref> Same year, ''[[BuzzFeed]]'' ranked it number 48 in their list of "The 101 Greatest Dance Songs of the '90s".<ref>{{Cite web|first1=Matt|last1=Stopera|first2=Brian|last2=Galindo|title=The 101 Greatest Dance Songs of the '90s|website=[[BuzzFeed]]|date=11 March 2017|access-date=31 March 2020|url=https://www.buzzfeed.com/mjs538/jump-to-the-rhythm-jump-jump-to-the-rhythm-jump|author-link=Matt Stopera}}</ref> In 2019, ''Billboard'' ranked it number 102 in their ranking of "''Billboard''{{'}}s Top Songs of the '90s"<ref name="billboardstopsongs90s"/> while in October 2023, it was ranked number 318 in their "500 Best Pop Songs of All Time".<ref name="billboard500bestpopsongs"/> In 2020, British footballer and MC [[Matt Robinson (footballer, born 1993)|Kamakaze]] (a.k.a. Matt Robinson) named it one of "The Best Tunes from the 90's", saying, "[[Leicester]]'s longest standing hold in pop music ever I think. Instant club banger anywhere or anytime."<ref>{{cite web|first=Felicity|last=Martin|url=https://dmy.co/10-best/10-best-tunes-90s-kamakaze|title=The 10 Best Tunes From The 90's, According To Kamakaze|publisher=DMY|date=28 February 2020|accessdate=24 February 2026}}</ref>

In April 2026, the song went viral on the platform [[TikTok]] when accompanying highlights of [[Paul George]], with some fans dubbing it the "unwashed anthem".
